## Verdict

- **Target `effect@4.1.2`** (npm `latest`, published 2026-11-02). Pin every `@effect/*` package to the same version. Effect 4 shipped as 4.0.0 on 2026-10-01 and is an LTS line. Do not start on 3.x.
- **Workers run the HttpApi module.** `HttpRouter.toWebHandler` is the first-party adapter, and its own API docs carry Cloudflare-specific instructions. A real HttpApi Worker bundles to about 86 KiB gzip and starts in about 55–60 ms of local CPU, against a 1 s limit (my measurements below).
- **First-party coverage stops at HTTP and SQL.** Effect ships `@effect/sql-d1` and `@effect/sql-sqlite-do`. It ships nothing for DO classes, Workflow entrypoints, Queues or bindings. You either write a thin bridge yourself, or use Alchemy v2 (`alchemy@2.0.0-beta.85`), which is Effect-native and already covers Workers, DOs, Workflows, D1, KV and Queues. SPEC already fixes Alchemy as the infrastructure tool.
- **Maturity risk is real but bounded.** Every module involved (`effect/http`, `effect/http-api`, `effect/sql`, `effect/workflow`, `effect/schema/Model`, and all `@effect/sql-*` drivers) is tagged `@stability unstable`. That tag allows breaking changes in minor releases. Several Workers-specific bugs were fixed in Sept–Oct 2026, and one fix for request scopes is still open. Pin exact versions and read changelogs before you bump.

## 1. Effect version and what changed in v4

| Fact | Source |
| --- | --- |
| `effect` dist-tags: `latest: 4.1.2`, `prev: 3.22.4`. 4.0.0 published 2026-10-01, 4.1.0 on 2026-10-29, 4.1.2 on 2026-11-02 | `npm view effect dist-tags time` |
| "Effect 4.x is a long-term support (LTS) release, with at least three years of bug and security fixes." Bug fixes until Sept 2029 or one year after 5.0, whichever is later | `effect@4.1.2` README; https://effect.website/blog/releases/effect/40 |
| v4 development moved from `Effect-TS/effect-smol` (now archived, "Effect V4 Has Moved") into `Effect-TS/effect` `main`. v3 lives on the `v3` branch | https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect-smol README |
| Minimal program: 3.x 35.6 kB vs 4.x 7.1 kB (min+gzip). Throughput 6.4× higher, 86 % less memory per fiber | https://effect.website/blog/releases/effect/40 |
| Requires TypeScript ≥ 5.9 and `strict`. Node ≥ 22.19 when running on Node | `effect@4.1.2` README |

What changed for the platform packages (https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/blob/main/MIGRATION.md):

- **`@effect/platform`, `@effect/rpc`, `@effect/cluster`, `@effect/sql` and others were merged into `effect`.** HTTP is now `effect/http` and HttpApi is now `effect/http-api`. SQL is `effect/sql`, workflows are `effect/workflow`, and so on. `@effect/platform` stays on its v3 line (`0.97.x`). Do not install it with v4.
- **Lockstep versioning.** Every remaining package (`@effect/platform-*`, `@effect/sql-*`, `@effect/ai-*`, `@effect/vitest`, `@effect/opentelemetry`) shares one version with `effect`.
- **Unstable module paths lost their `unstable` segment.** Use `effect/http`, not `effect/unstable/http`, and no compatibility exports remain. The modules are still `@stability unstable`, which means "new features in patch releases and breaking changes in minor releases". The migration guide also says "Moving these modules does not stabilize their APIs." The unstable list includes `http`, `http-api`, `rpc`, `schema` (sub-modules such as `Model`), `sql` and `workflow`. Every module in packages other than `effect` is unstable too.
- Core renames that affect every file: `Context.Tag` → `Context.Service`, `Schema.TaggedError` keeps its name, `catch*` combinators were renamed, and `Runtime<R>` was removed. The links are in MIGRATION.md.
- There is no `@effect/platform-cloudflare` and no `@effect/cloudflare` package (both 404 on npm). Workers use the platform-neutral `effect/http` directly.

### The adapter

v3's `HttpApp.toWebHandler` / `HttpApiBuilder.toWebHandler` became `HttpRouter.toWebHandler(appLayer, options)` in v4. It returns `{ handler, dispose }`, where `handler(request, context?)` returns a `Promise<Response>`. Its JSDoc in `effect@4.1.2` (`dist/http/HttpRouter.d.ts`) has a Cloudflare section:

## 4. Local dev mode

- `alchemy dev` (default stage `dev_$USER`) runs Workers in **workerd directly**, with Alchemy's own simulators in `@alchemy.run/cloudflare-runtime`. **It is not Miniflare.** Miniflare appears only in Alchemy's private test tools. SPEC §6.3's "Miniflare, through Alchemy's dev mode" is slightly off: the emulation is workerd-based, but it is not Miniflare. v1 did use Miniflare (`alchemy-async/alchemy/src/cloudflare/miniflare/`). Source: https://alchemy.run/cloudflare/local-development, src: `packages/cloudflare-runtime/package.json` (depends on `workerd`, not `miniflare`).
- **Emulated locally:** Workers (with hot reload), Durable Objects including SQLite, KV, R2 (plus an S3 endpoint), D1 (migrations applied on every reconcile), Queues + consumers (batching, retry, **dead-letter semantics**), Workflows ("real step semantics"), Secrets Store (seeded with real values), and Vite and other framework dev servers with HMR. Crons fire on schedule, and `/cdn-cgi/handler/scheduled` triggers them manually. Email `send_email` writes `.eml` files, and `POST /cdn-cgi/handler/email` drives inbound mail.
- **Not emulated:** Workers AI is a remote binding (real calls, billed). Analytics Engine is a no-op stub. Turnstile has no simulator. DNS and Vectorize deploy to the cloud in your personal stage.
- `Alchemy.remote()` opts a single resource out of emulation, for example a real queue or real email. Moving a resource between local and live plans a **replacement**.
- Open issues: #2810 (mixing local and remote is hard to get right), #2884 (local R2 S3 credentials are rejected by S3 clients), #2879 (binding clients fail when the env name differs from the logical ID).

## 5. Vitest integration

- `@alchemy.run/test` provides `Test.make({ providers, state, stage, dev })` with adapters for `alchemy-test`, `bun test` and **Vitest** (`@alchemy.run/test/Vitest` + `@effect/vitest`, where each test is an `it.live`). `deploy(Stack)` / `destroy(Stack)` run the real stack. **`dev: true` runs it against the local workerd simulators instead of the cloud.** The test stage defaults to `test_$USER`, or set `ALCHEMY_TEST_STAGE=ci-pr-42`. Sources: https://alchemy.run/testing/test-harness, https://alchemy.run/testing/testing-a-stack, https://alchemy.run/cloudflare/tutorial/part-4
- **Gap:** tests run in Node (or Bun) and drive the stack over HTTP or RPC. This is integration-style testing. Alchemy has **no integration with `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers`**: no grep hits in the repo, and no wrangler-config generator in v2 (v1 had `WranglerJson`). To unit-test DO or adapter code inside the isolate (calling `runInDurableObject` or reading storage directly), you would need a separate test-only wrangler config for vitest-pool-workers, which works against SPEC's "no hand-edited wrangler config". **Workaround (recommended):** keep domain logic in plain Node tests, as SPEC already requires. Test the adapters through `Test.make({ dev: true })` against small test-only RPC methods or HTTP routes in the stack. Run a smaller `Test.make()` cloud smoke test on the PR stage.

## 6. Gaps and workarounds (summary)
### Alchemy v2: Effect-native Cloudflare runtime

`alchemy@2.0.0-beta.85` and `@alchemy.run/cloudflare@2.0.0-beta.85` (2026-11-02) have a peer dependency on `effect ^4.1.0`. They define Workers, DOs and Workflows as Effect classes, with bindings resolved as Effect services (https://github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy, `packages/cloudflare/src/Workers`, `.../Workflows`):

- `Cloudflare.Worker<Api>()("Api", { main: import.meta.url }, Effect.gen(...))` returns `{ fetch: Effect }`. The init Effect pulls bindings (`yield* Cloudflare.D1.QueryDatabase(Db)`, `yield* Cloudflare.KV.ReadWriteNamespace(KV)`). The demo `demos/effect-prezzy/chapters/02-d1/src/Api.ts` serves an `HttpApiBuilder.layer(ShortyApi)` this way, through `HttpRouter.toHttpEffect`.
- `Cloudflare.DurableObject<Users>()("Users", Effect.gen(...))` returns typed RPC methods. Callers use `users.getByName(id).listUsers()` (`examples/cloudflare-durable-object-sql`). Migrations come from `Cloudflare.SqlMigrations`.
- `Cloudflare.Workflow<NotifyWorkflow>()("Notifier", ...)` with `Cloudflare.Workflows.task("name", effect, { retries, timeout, rollback })` wraps `step.do` and threads services into each step (`examples/cloudflare-worker/src/NotifyWorkflow.ts`). Alchemy also implements `effect/workflow`'s `WorkflowEngine` on native Workflows (`NativeEngine.ts`) and on Durable Objects (`DurableObjectEngine.ts`).
- Alchemy files Workers-runtime bugs upstream and fixes them, for example #10364 above and [alchemy#1639](https://github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy/pull/1639) (merged 2026-11-04).

Trade-off: Alchemy's runtime layer reduces the bridge code to almost nothing, and it matches the SPEC's choice of IaC tool. But it is beta (85 betas, a release every 1–2 weeks), so it couples app runtime code to the IaC tool's release cadence. The domain package stays clean either way, because it depends only on `effect`. Decide this in the architecture ticket. Keep adapters thin, so that moving between the plain bridge and Alchemy's runtime only touches the adapters package.

## 4. Bundle size and cold start (measured)

I measured this on 2026-11-07 with `effect@4.1.2`, `rolldown@1.2.13` (the bundler Alchemy uses), `esbuild@0.25.10` and `wrangler@4.158.0` on linux. The Worker serves an `HttpApi` with one group, three endpoints (GET list, GET by id with a typed 404 error, POST with a Schema payload) and an env-backed service, set up as in §2. The client calls `HttpApiClient.make(Api)` with `FetchHttpClient`. The scripts are in the scratchpad and are not committed. Rerun them by bundling the snippet in §2.

| Bundle | rolldown min | rolldown gzip | esbuild min | esbuild gzip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal `Effect.runPromise(Effect.succeed(1))` | 23.5 KB | 8.4 KB | 167 KB (barrel import) / 27 KB (`effect/Effect` import) | 58 KB / 9.9 KB |
| HttpApi Worker (server) | 275 KB | 87.5 KB | 521 KB | 169 KB |
| HttpApi typed client (browser) | 190 KB | 59.4 KB | 426 KB | 138 KB |

- **Bundler matters.** esbuild did not tree-shake `import { Effect } from "effect"` barrel namespaces, so its bundles came out 2–7× larger. Rolldown (Vite 8, Alchemy) matched the 7.1 kB headline. If anything uses esbuild, import from deep paths (`effect/Effect`).
- **Worker limits** are 64 MiB uncompressed with no compressed limit, and global scope must finish within 1 s (https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/limits/). An 87 KB-gzip Worker is far below both.
- **Startup.** `wrangler check startup` reported 53.9 / 58.4 / 61.0 ms active startup CPU across three runs for the HttpApi Worker, against 0–10 ms for a hello-world Worker. That is local workerd, and Cloudflare warns production CPUs differ. In Node 26: 37–43 ms module evaluation, about 45–50 ms for the first request (the layer was already built), and about 120–140 µs per warm request.
- **Verified behaviour** in the same run: 200 with JSON for list. 404 `{"_tag":"PulseNotFound","id":"2"}` for the typed error. 400 `HttpApiSchemaError` for a bad payload.
- **Answer page (SPEC §6.1):** the typed client costs about 59 KB gzip before any app code. For the small answer-page entry, either accept that or call the two or three answer endpoints with plain `fetch` plus the shared Schemas. Schema alone is far smaller than the HttpApi client. Measure this when the entry exists.

## 5. Effect Schema with SQLite (DO `sql` and D1)

- **`@effect/sql-sqlite-do@4.1.2`**: `SqliteClient.layer({ db?: SqlStorage, storage?: DurableObjectStorage })` provides `SqliteClient` and the generic `SqlClient`. Pass `storage` (not just `db`) to get transactions and migrations. "Transactions use `storage.transaction()` instead of transaction SQL." Nested transactions roll back on their own. Blobs come back as `Uint8Array`, and `updateValues` is unsupported. `SqliteMigrator.run/layer` records applied migrations in `effect_sql_migrations` and is meant to run "during construction" of the DO (package JSDoc, `dist/SqliteClient.d.ts`, `dist/SqliteMigrator.d.ts`).
- **`@effect/sql-d1@4.1.2`**: `D1Client.layer({ db: D1Database })`. It caches prepared statements and maps failures to `SqlError`. **No transactions, no streaming, no `updateValues`** (package JSDoc). That fits SPEC's small global index, but multi-row invariants need D1 `batch()` or a design that avoids them.
- **Schema ↔ SQL**: `effect/schema/Model` (`Model.Class` with `select`/`insert`/`update`/`json`/`jsonCreate`/`jsonUpdate` variants) plus `effect/sql` `SqlSchema` and `SqlModel` give one schema per domain type, shared by the API (`User.json` in the HttpApi fixtures) and the database. SPEC §6.1 asks for exactly this. All of it is `@stability unstable`.
- **DO SQLite limits to design around**: 100 bound parameters per query, 100 KB per statement, 2 MB per row, 100 columns, 10 GB per object on Workers Paid (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/platform/limits/). Effect's own `SqlEventJournal` chunks at 100 parameters for this reason (`effect/src/eventlog/SqlEventJournal.ts`). Bulk inserts must chunk.
- **DO write-coalescing caveat**: Cloudflare commits writes with no intervening `await` atomically, and `sql.exec()` is synchronous (https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/). Effect's async scheduler can put a macrotask between two statements, so use `withTransaction` explicitly for multi-statement invariants rather than relying on coalescing.

## 6. Testing with swapped layers in plain Node

- `@effect/vitest@4.1.2` provides `it.effect` and `layer(TestLayer)("suite", (it) => ...)`.
- `effect/http-api` `HttpApiTest.groups(Api, ["users"])` builds a typed client wired directly to the handlers, with no server and no network, "using the same request encoding, routing, and response decoding as a real server". The published example (`ai-docs/src/51_http-server/20_testing.ts`) swaps `Users.layerMemory` in for the SQL-backed layer and swaps auth middleware per test. This is exactly the plain-Node domain/API testing that SPEC §6.3 asks for.
- Because `toWebHandler` returns a plain `(Request) => Promise<Response>`, the same Worker entry can also be smoke-tested in Node with `new Request(...)`. I did this in §4.
- Adapter tests (DO SQLite, D1, Workflows) still need workerd: `@cloudflare/vitest-pool-workers` or Alchemy's local dev. `cloudflare:workers` `withEnv` overrides imported `env` in tests.

## 7. Examples in the wild

- **Alchemy v2** examples and demos (first-party, maintained, Effect 4): `examples/cloudflare-effect-sql-d1`, `examples/cloudflare-durable-object-sql`, `examples/cloudflare-worker` (Worker + DO + Workflow + Queue + KV), `examples/cloudflare-federated-api` (HttpApi), `demos/effect-prezzy` (HttpApi + D1 + Queues chapters). https://github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy/tree/main/examples
- **danieljvdm/effect-cf**: "Effect-native primitives for Cloudflare Workers and bindings", Effect ^4.1, 116 stars, active (pushed 2026-10-29). https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-cf
- **gjermundgaraba/effect-actions PR #51**: Effect RPC served from Durable Objects over hibernating WebSockets. https://github.com/gjermundgaraba/effect-actions/pull/51
- **deracs/create-effect-project**: Effect v4 scaffolder with a Cloudflare Worker template for HTTP or RPC. https://github.com/deracs/create-effect-project
- **ksamirdev/effect-rpc-workers**: `@effect/rpc` on Workers. Last pushed 2025-12, before v4 shipped, so use it only for the pattern. https://github.com/ksamirdev/effect-rpc-workers
- Sandro Maglione, "Effect API on Cloudflare" (v3 `HttpApiBuilder.toWebHandler`, a secondary source). https://www.sandromaglione.com/newsletter/effect-api-on-cloudflare

## Recommendations for the build

1. Pin `effect`, `@effect/sql-sqlite-do`, `@effect/sql-d1`, `@effect/vitest` (and `@effect/ai-cloudflare` if used) to exactly `4.1.2`, and bump them together.
2. Build the HttpApi handler once at module scope with `MixedScheduler("sync")`. Pass `env`/`ctx` per request as a `Context`. Allow no shared background fibers.
3. Domain services depend on domain interfaces. Adapters provide them from `CfEnv`, DO `storage` or D1. Tests swap in memory layers and use `HttpApiTest`.
4. Decide in the architecture ticket whether to use Alchemy v2's Effect runtime (`Cloudflare.Worker/DurableObject/Workflow`) or a hand-written bridge of about 100 lines. Both work on 4.1.x.
5. Write a spike before committing: one org DO with `SqliteClient` + `withTransaction` + migrations, one Workflow with two `step.do` Effects, deployed to a preview stage. Measure deployed cold start there, since local CPU numbers do not carry over.

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

I've claimed **[How is the codebase laid out and which tools does it use?](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/issues/17)** and re-read the Alchemy and Effect research. The relevant facts:

- **Alchemy v2 beta 85** ties itself to Effect 4.
- **Version pinning:** Effect 4.1.2's HTTP and SQL modules are marked unstable, so both libraries need exact pins.
- **Bundling:** rolldown builds a much smaller bundle than esbuild.
- **Tests:** there is no `vitest-pool-workers`. Alchemy's `Test.make({ dev: true })` runs the stack on local workerd instead.

Round 1:

---

❓ **Q1** - **Package manager and runtime versions**:

➡️ Use **pnpm workspaces with a `catalog:`** that pins exact versions: `effect` and every `@effect/*` package at **4.1.2**, plus `alchemy` and `@alchemy.run/*` at **2.0.0-beta.85**. They're bumped only together, in a PR of their own. Node **24 LTS**, pinned in `.node-version`, with mise reading that file. Alchemy's own repo uses pnpm and a catalog in the same way.

---

❓ **Q2** - **How Effect reaches Cloudflare**: The options are:
- (a) **Alchemy v2's Effect runtime**: `Cloudflare.Worker`, `Cloudflare.DurableObject`, Queue consumers and `cron` are defined as Effects, and their bindings are typed services.
- (b) A **hand-written bridge** of about 100 lines over plain `DurableObject` and `fetch` classes. It doesn't depend on Alchemy's beta release pace.

➡️ **(a)**, but only inside the adapters package, so the domain package never imports Alchemy. If the beta lets us down, moving to (b) means rewriting only that package. Before slicing, a **spike task** proves the choice on a preview stage. The spike covers:
- an Organization DO using `SqliteClient`, `withTransaction`, migrations and an alarm;
- a Queue consumer with a dead-letter queue;
- the Submission Worker with every log setting off;
- the deployed cold start.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Packages**:

➡️ Six packages:
- `packages/domain`: pure Effect. Schemas, services, the privacy rules, schedule calculations and Result calculations, organised by concept (`people/`, `pulses/`, `rounds/`, `answering/`, `results/`, `actions/`, `privacy/`). Its only dependency is `effect`.
- `packages/api`: the HttpApi declaration, shared by server and client. It depends on `domain`.
- `packages/cloudflare`: the adapters (the Organization DO, D1, the Queue consumer, `EmailSender`, the alarm scheduler) and the **two Worker entries**, the main Worker and the Submission Worker.
- `apps/web`: a Vite 8 project with **two entries**. One is the app (React, TanStack Router, Base UI). The other is the **answer page**, which must not import React or the HttpApi client. It uses plain `fetch` and shared Schemas. Its framework is decided in the answer-page fog.
- `packages/emails`: the email templates.
- `infra`: the Alchemy stack, with stages for `pr-<n>`, `staging` and `production`.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Test layers and runners**:

➡️ **Vitest with `@effect/vitest` everywhere**, in four layers:
- **Domain and API tests** run in plain Node with in-memory layers, and API tests use `HttpApiTest`.
- **Adapter tests** use `@alchemy.run/test` `Test.make({ dev: true })` against local workerd, driving the stack through small test-only RPC methods.
- **Preview-stage smoke tests** use `Test.make()` against the PR stage.
- **End-to-end tests** run Playwright against the PR stage.

`vitest-pool-workers` isn't used, and there's no hand-edited wrangler config.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Lint, format and the domain boundary**:

➡️ **Biome** handles formatting and general lint. The `@effect/language-service` TS plugin reports Effect diagnostics. **The domain boundary is enforced by dependencies, not by a lint rule:**
- `domain` lists only `effect` as a dependency, so with pnpm's strict layout any other import fails to resolve;
- its tsconfig has `types: []`, so no `@cloudflare/workers-types` globals are visible;
- a CI check fails if `domain` or `api` ever import `cloudflare:*` or `alchemy`.

The privacy query lint (A3) is a small **custom script** that scans SQL in the adapters package. Biome's plugin support is too limited for it, so the script runs in CI next to Biome.

---

❓ **Q6** - **TypeScript settings**:

➡️ TypeScript **5.9** (the version Effect 4 requires), with:
- `strict`, `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`, `verbatimModuleSyntax`, `moduleResolution: "bundler"` and `isolatedDeclarations: false`;
- **project references** between packages and `tsc -b` in CI.

No `any`, and no `as` outside tests. Testing `tsgo` comes later.

---

❓ **Q7** - **What gets scaffolded first**:

➡️ A **walking skeleton** as the first implementation issue. It contains:
- the six packages with their boundaries;
- an Alchemy stack with both Workers, the Organization DO, D1 and one Queue;
- CI that runs typecheck, Biome, unit tests and an adapter test, and deploys `pr-<n>` on each PR and destroys it when the PR closes;
- one endpoint that runs end to end (create an Organization → read it back) through domain, API, adapter and DO.

Every other implementation issue builds on that skeleton. The spike from Q2 runs first, and its findings feed the skeleton.

---

Answer by number, or "yes to all".

content.text:
You're right, 5.9 was a mistake on my part. I took Effect's stated minimum and didn't check what has shipped since. Here is what the registry and the package files show today:

| | Fact |
| --- | --- |
| `typescript` on npm | `latest` is **7.0.2**, released 2026-07-08. This is the native Go compiler. 6.0.3 (April 2026) was the last release written in JavaScript. 7.1 is in beta. |
| Effect 4.1.2 README | "TypeScript 5.9 or newer. **TypeScript 7 is recommended** for the best performance and compatibility with Effect's TypeScript tooling." |
| Effect's editor tooling | The `@effect/language-service` README says: "If you are using TypeScript 7.0 or newer, use **`@effect/tsgo`** instead." `@effect/tsgo` is at 0.67.4, published 2026-11-06. |
| Alchemy v2 beta 85 | `alchemy` and `@alchemy.run/cloudflare` are developed against `typescript ^7.0.2`. |

TypeScript 7 doesn't keep the old JavaScript compiler API, so tools built on that API may break. Our stack doesn't depend on it:
- Biome has its own parser.
- Vite 8 and rolldown strip types without running `tsc`.
- Vitest uses oxc.

The only place we needed TypeScript's API was Effect's diagnostics, and `@effect/tsgo` replaces that. TypeScript 6 would be the worst of both: it's the end of the old compiler line, and Effect's tooling no longer favours it.

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

I've claimed **[What does Release 1's rule-based comment redaction remove, and how is it proven?](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/issues/20)**. ADR 0001 already settles that the Lead reads redacted comments only once the Round meets N, and that members see no comments. Round 1:

---

❓ **Q1** - **Which names count**: The Organization's roster is the only list of names we have. Scenarios to consider:
- "Will" or "May", first names that are also ordinary words;
- "José" written as "Jose";
- "Bob" for a Robert, which is a nickname;
- "Peter from the client", who isn't in the roster at all.

➡️ Redact every Person in the Organization: their first name, last name, full name and the local part of their email address. Matching ignores case, Unicode width and accents, and works on whole words using `Intl.Segmenter`, so "Anna's" matches "Anna". Names shorter than 2 characters are ignored. **Names that are also ordinary words are redacted anyway**: "I will" becomes "I [name]". We accept the false positives, because missing a real name is worse than an odd sentence. **No nickname list and no names outside the roster in R1.** The disclosure says exactly that, so we don't overclaim.

---

❓ **Q2** - **Other patterns**:

➡️ Also redact:
- **email addresses** → `[email]`;
- **phone numbers**, meaning runs of 7 or more digits with common separators → `[phone]`;
- **@handles** → `[handle]`;
- **every URL**, because URLs often contain names or profile ids → `[link]`.

Names become `[name]`. Plain numbers like "3 people" or "2 weeks" stay.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Placeholder or holding the whole comment**:

➡️ **A placeholder per match**, using the tokens above. A comment is never held back as a whole. Redaction never covers what SPEC calls "unusual identifying phrases", such as "as the only designer". That needs the AI pass in R2, and the disclosure says so.

---

❓ **Q4** - **When redaction happens, and whether the raw text is kept**: If raw text is kept and redaction runs when the comment is shown, deleting a Person would remove their name from the roster, and old comments would start showing it. If redaction runs when the comment is stored, the original text is gone for good.

➡️ **Redact at store time, using the roster as it is at that moment, and store only the redacted text.** The raw text exists only in the Submission Worker's memory during that one request. It is never logged, never sent to an AI model in R1, and never stored, so a later roster change can never expose it. When the member edits a comment, they edit the redacted version. People added to the roster later are not redacted from older comments. We accept that.

---

❓ **Q5** - **What the member sees**: SPEC requires the answer page to state what the Lead will see.

➡️ Comments are saved as soon as they are given, like every other Answer. The save response returns the redacted text, and the page shows it right under the field: **"Your Lead will see: …"**. The member can edit it until close. Next to the first comment field, the page says:

> *"Your Lead reads comments word for word, once at least 4 people answer. We remove names of people in your organization, email addresses, phone numbers, handles and links. We don't remove other details, so leave out anything that identifies you."*

---

❓ **Q6** - **Length and where the code lives**:

➡️ Comments have a **1,000-character limit**, counted after Unicode normalisation. Redaction is a **pure function in `packages/domain/privacy`**, `redact(text, roster) → redacted`, with no Cloudflare imports. It's fully unit-testable and is part of the privacy suite.

---

❓ **Q7** - **Test cases that prove it**:

➡️ A table-driven test in the privacy suite covers:
- case and accents ("anna", "ANNA", "Ánna");
- possessives ("Anna's");
- full names spanning two words ("Mary Ann Lee");
- ordinary words that are also roster names ("will" when Will is in the roster);
- an email address, phone numbers in five formats, an @handle, and a URL that contains a name;
- names glued to punctuation ("(Anna)");
- a name that is a substring of another word: "Ann" inside "annual" stays.

A property test checks that **no roster name ever survives in the output** for randomly generated sentences. A separate test checks that **the stored value equals the redacted value**, and that no log line or response contains the raw text.

---

Answer by number, or "yes to all".
yes to all

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

I've claimed **[How is the privacy test suite built and run?](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/issues/25)**. The rules it has to cover are already fixed:
- the 11 minimum-group-size rules (R1–R11);
- the storage invariants A1–A10;
- the redaction cases.

What's open is where each check runs and what blocks what. Round 1:

---

❓ **Q1** - **Which layer each check runs in**:

➡️ Each check runs at the cheapest layer that can actually prove it:

| Layer | Checks |
| --- | --- |
| **Domain, plain Node** | Minimum group size rules R1–R11 as pure functions over Result inputs, `redact`, A8 (double submission rejected) and A9 (Person deletion), both against in-memory layers |
| **API, `HttpApiTest` in Node** | Every endpoint that returns Result data obeys R1–R11 for Leads and members. A5 (token plus Edit key rejected). An Open Round returns only counts. Comments never come back with ratings or Submission ids |
| **Lint, oxlint plugin** | A3 (query rules) and the import boundary |
| **Adapter, `Test.make({ dev: true })` on workerd** | A1 and A2 schema checks on the migrated Durable Object (`sqlite_master`/`PRAGMA`: `WITHOUT ROWID`, no forbidden columns), A4 unlinkability on real SQLite, A8 inside a real transaction, A10 backup order, stored comment equals redacted comment |
| **Preview stage** | A6 (the token never reaches the main Worker), A7 (the Submission Worker produces no logs or events), and a canary sweep (Q3) |

---

❓ **Q2** - **Making A4 ("no better than chance") reliable**: A statistical test on random keys can fail by bad luck.

➡️ **Make the randomness deterministic.** Keys come from Effect's `Random` service, which the test seeds. The test then writes k = 200 Submissions in a known order and runs each attack we can name against the dump:
- matching by rank;
- matching by key order;
- matching on any shared column value;
- matching on `rowid` where one exists.

It asserts that **each attack's match rate is at most 2/k**. It runs with **three fixed seeds**. With fixed seeds the result is the same on every run, so it never fails at random. It still fails for real if a code change brings back an ordering, because then the attacks start matching.

---

❓ **Q3** - **Proving that nothing leaks into logs or other sinks**: Cloudflare doesn't publish the full field list of an invocation log, so checking only the fields we know about isn't enough.

➡️ Use a **canary sweep on the preview stage**. The test creates an Organization whose Person email, Invitation token, comment text and Edit key are unique canary strings. It then runs the full flow: invite, answer, comment, close, view Results. After that it **searches every sink for each canary**:
- Workers Logs through the Observability API (all Workers);
- Analytics Engine through its SQL API;
- Queue and dead-letter messages, captured by a test consumer;
- R2 backup objects;
- a D1 dump;
- every HTTP response body the Lead and members received.

The expected result is **zero hits**, except the redacted comment text in the Lead's Results view. The Submission Worker must also show **zero events of any kind** (A7). The search keeps retrying for up to 10 minutes, because logs arrive late.

---

❓ **Q4** - **No Result view can skip the rules**: Someone adds an endpoint later and forgets the group-size check.

➡️ A **registry test**. It lists every HttpApi endpoint from the `api` declaration, and every endpoint whose response schema contains Result data must appear in a privacy table, with a generator for its inputs. An unlisted endpoint fails CI. For each listed endpoint, a **property test** generates Rounds (Submission counts, skipped Questions, N values, history, raising and lowering N) and asserts:
- no aggregate with fewer Contributors than the effective N appears;
- each Dimension value equals the mean of the Questions shown.

---

❓ **Q5** - **What blocks a merge and what blocks a release**:

➡️
- **Every PR:** the domain, API, lint and adapter layers are required checks in one CI job called **`privacy`**.
- **PRs that touch `packages/cloudflare`, `infra` or the answer page:** the preview-stage checks are required too (A6, A7 and the canary sweep).
- **Production deploys:** they need a green preview-stage `privacy` run on `staging` for that exact commit.
- **Release checklist (not CI):** a manual send to a Microsoft 365 tenant with Defender switched on. It's done before the first external Organization and again when the email or answer flow changes.

---

❓ **Q6** - **Where the tests live**:

➡️ They live **next to the code they test**, named `*.privacy.test.ts`. `pnpm test:privacy` runs them across all packages. The preview-stage checks live in `infra/tests/privacy/`. Exports and the MCP server come after R1, and the registry from Q4 is where their checks will go when they arrive.

---

Answer by number, or "yes to all".
yes to all

| "Submission Worker produces zero events" (A7) | **INCONCLUSIVE**, see finding 2 |

| Per-PR stage from GitHub Actions | **Not tested.** It needs a Cloudflare API token as a repo secret, so it moves to the CI pipeline work |

**Findings that change later work**
1. **Alchemy doesn't apply every observability prop.** The code set `logs.invocationLogs: false` and `persist: false`. The deployed Submission Worker had `observability.enabled=false` and `logs.enabled=false`, but `invocation_logs=true` and `persist=true`. Alchemy also turns logs *on* when `observability` is omitted. So the privacy suite must **read the deployed settings back from the Cloudflare API** on every preview and staging deploy and fail on any field that isn't off. Config in code is not enough.
2. **The canary sweep needs a positive control.** Over 12+ minutes, the Observability API returned zero events for *both* spike Workers, including the Main Worker, which has logs on. The same query saw another Worker on the account. Until a known-logging Worker's canary shows up, "zero hits" proves nothing. The sweep (and A7) must first assert that the Main Worker's canary *is* found, then that nothing else is. 3. **First activation of an Organization DO costs about 0.5 s** (creation plus migrations). That's fine for Organization creation, but the answer path must never be the first touch of a cold object. The Submission Worker reaches an object that already exists, so this holds in R1.
4. **Bundle size roughly doubles with Alchemy's runtime.** It's well within Worker limits, but the Submission Worker should stay minimal (minified, no HttpApi server if a plain router is enough) to protect the 300 ms p95 submit budget. That belongs with the answer-page work.

The spike is done, and **[Spike: Alchemy v2 Effect runtime on a preview stage](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/issues/29)** is closed. I deployed the `spike29` stage to `*.workers.dev`, ran the checks, and destroyed it: all 6 resources are deleted, and no `spike29` Worker is left. The throwaway code and evidence are on the unmerged branch [`spike/alchemy-runtime`](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/tree/spike/alchemy-runtime).

**ADR 0008 holds.** On real Cloudflare:
- **Organization DO:** the table has no row ids and `SELECT rowid` fails. Transactions roll back, both migration paths run, and the alarm re-arms.
- **API:** the HttpApi request goes from the Worker to the DO and back.
- **Queues:** the Queue and its dead-letter queue both work.
- **Tooling:** TypeScript 7 project builds, `@effect/tsgo` and the oxlint plugin rule all work.

Four findings change later work:
1. **Alchemy doesn't fully switch off logging.** On the deployed Submission Worker, the master switch and logs are off. But `invocation_logs` and `persist` stayed **on**, even though the code sets both off. The privacy suite will read the deployed settings back from the Cloudflare API after every preview and staging deploy, and fail on anything that should be off.
2. **The "zero logs" check proved nothing yet.** For 12+ minutes the Observability API showed zero events for *both* Workers, including the Main Worker, which has logs on and served about 25 requests. Another Worker on your account shows up fine. So the log search (the canary sweep) now has to find the Main Worker's logs first, before an empty result from the Submission Worker counts. Why the new Workers' logs never appeared is still open. I put it under "CI and preview pipeline" on the map.
3. **A new Organization costs about 0.5 s on its first request**, because the DO is created and migrated. A warm request is 66 ms. The answer path always reaches an object that already exists, so the answer page isn't affected.
4. **The bundles are about twice the size the research measured**: Main 192 KiB, Submission 137 KiB gzip. I passed this to the answer-page ticket, since it bears on the 300 ms submit budget.

The per-PR stage from GitHub Actions **wasn't tested**, because it needs a Cloudflare API token as a repo secret. That now sits with the CI pipeline work.

The resolution comment has the full table. I added a follow-up on the privacy test suite ticket covering the settings read-back and the check that the Main Worker's logs appear first, and put a Decisions-so-far entry on the map.

Only **[How is the answer page built to load in under 1 second?](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/issues/30)** (prototype) is left on the frontier. After it, **Slice Release 1 into implementation issues** unblocks.

Base directory for this skill: /home/ubuntu/.claude/skills/prototype

# Prototype

A prototype is **throwaway code that answers a question**. The question decides the shape.

## Pick a branch

Identify which question is being answered, using the user's prompt, the surrounding code, or by asking if the user is around:

- **"Does this logic / state model feel right?"** → [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md). Build a single shareable HTML file (free-play buttons plus tabbed guided walkthroughs) that pushes the state machine through cases that are hard to reason about on paper, and that a non-developer can drive.
- **"What should this look like?"** → [UI.md](UI.md). Generate several radically different UI variations on a single route, switchable via a URL search param and a floating bottom bar.

The two branches produce very different artifacts, so getting this wrong wastes the whole prototype. If the question is genuinely ambiguous and the user isn't reachable, default to whichever branch better matches the surrounding code (a backend module → logic; a page or component → UI) and state the assumption at the top of the prototype.

## Rules that apply to both

1. **Throwaway from day one, and clearly marked as such.** Locate the prototype code close to where it will actually be used (next to the module or page it's prototyping for) so context is obvious, but name it so a casual reader can see it's a prototype, not production. For throwaway UI routes, obey whatever routing convention the project already uses; don't invent a new top-level structure.
2. **Trivial to run.** A UI prototype starts from one command in the project's task runner: `pnpm <name>`, `python <path>`, `bun <path>`, etc. A logic demo is a single HTML file the user double-clicks. Either way, no thinking required to start it.
3. **No persistence by default.** State lives in memory. Persistence is the thing the prototype is _checking_, not something it should depend on. If the question explicitly involves a database, hit a scratch DB or a local file with a clear "PROTOTYPE, wipe me" name.
4. **Skip the polish.** No tests, no error handling beyond what makes the prototype _runnable_, no abstractions. The point is to learn something fast.
5. **Surface the state.** After every action (logic) or on every variant switch (UI), print or render the full relevant state so the user can see what changed.
6. **Capture it when done.** Fold any validated decision into the real code, then capture the prototype itself as a **primary source**: commit it to a throwaway branch, out of main, and leave a context pointer to that branch on the implementation issue. Capture the answer too (the verdict and the question it settled) in the issue or a commit. The main branch keeps only the validated decision.

# UI Prototype

Generate **several radically different UI variations** on a single route, switchable from a floating bottom bar. The user flips between variants in the browser, picks one (or steals bits from each), then throws the rest away.

If the question is about logic/state rather than what something looks like, this is the wrong branch. Use [LOGIC.md](LOGIC.md).

## When this is the right shape

- "What should this page look like?"
- "I want to see a few options for this dashboard before committing."
- "Try a different layout for the settings screen."
- Any time the user would otherwise spend a day picking between three vague mockups in their head.

## Two sub-shapes: strongly prefer sub-shape A

A UI prototype is much easier to judge when it's **butting up against the rest of the app**: real header, real sidebar, real data, real density. A throwaway route on its own is a vacuum: every variant looks fine in isolation. Default to sub-shape A whenever there's a plausible existing page to host the variants. Only reach for sub-shape B if the prototype genuinely has no nearby home.

### Sub-shape A: adjustment to an existing page (preferred)

The route already exists. Variants are rendered **on the same route**, gated by a `?variant=` URL search param. The existing data fetching, params, and auth all stay. Only the rendering swaps. This is the default; pick it unless there's a specific reason not to.

If the prototype is for something that doesn't yet have a page but *would naturally live inside one* (a new section of the dashboard, a new card on the settings screen, a new step in an existing flow), it's still sub-shape A. Mount the variants inside the host page.

### Sub-shape B: a new page (last resort)

Only use this when the thing being prototyped genuinely has no existing page to live inside (e.g. an entirely new top-level surface, or a flow that can't be embedded anywhere sensible).

Create a **throwaway route** following whatever routing convention the project already uses. Don't invent a new top-level structure. Name it so it's obviously a prototype (e.g. include the word `prototype` in the path or filename). Same `?variant=` pattern.

Before committing to sub-shape B, sanity-check: is there really no existing page this could be embedded in? An empty route hides design problems that a populated one would expose.

In both sub-shapes the floating bottom bar is identical.

## Process

### 1. State the question and pick N

Default to **3 variants**. More than 5 stops being radically different and starts being noise, so cap there.

Write down the plan in one line, in the prototype's location or a top-of-file comment:

> "Three variants of the settings page, switchable via `?variant=`, on the existing `/settings` route."

This works whether the user is here to push back or not.

### 2. Generate radically different variants

Draft each variant. Hold each one to:

- The page's purpose and the data it has access to.
- The project's component library / styling system (TailwindCSS, shadcn, MUI, plain CSS, whatever).
- A clear exported component name, e.g. `VariantA`, `VariantB`, `VariantC`.

Variants must be **structurally different**: different layout, different information hierarchy, different primary affordance, not just different colours. Three slightly-tweaked card grids isn't a UI prototype, it's wallpaper. If two drafts come out too similar, redo one with explicit "do not use a card grid" guidance.

### 3. Wire them together

Create a single switcher component on the route:

```tsx
// pseudo-code, adapt to the project's framework
const variant = searchParams.get('variant') ?? 'A';
return (
  <>
    {variant === 'A' && <VariantA {...data} />}
    {variant === 'B' && <VariantB {...data} />}
    {variant === 'C' && <VariantC {...data} />}
    <PrototypeSwitcher variants={['A','B','C']} current={variant} />
  </>
);
```

For sub-shape A (existing page): keep all the existing data fetching above the switcher; only the rendered subtree changes per variant.

For sub-shape B (new page): the throwaway route under `/prototype/<name>` mounts the same switcher.

### 4. Build the floating switcher

A small fixed-position bar at the bottom-centre of the screen with three pieces:

- **Left arrow**: cycles to the previous variant (wraps around).
- **Variant label**: shows the current variant key and, if the variant exports a name, that name too. e.g. `B (Sidebar layout)`.
- **Right arrow**: cycles forward (wraps around).

Behaviour:

- Clicking an arrow updates the URL search param (use the framework's router, e.g. `router.replace` on Next, `navigate` on React Router, etc) so the variant is shareable and reload-stable.
- Keyboard: `←` and `→` arrow keys also cycle. Don't intercept arrow keys when an `<input>`, `<textarea>`, or `[contenteditable]` is focused.
- Visually distinct from the page (e.g. high-contrast pill, subtle shadow) so it's obviously not part of the design being evaluated.
- Hidden in production builds: gate on `process.env.NODE_ENV !== 'production'` or an equivalent check, so a stray prototype merge can't ship the bar to users.

Put the switcher in a single shared component so both sub-shapes can reuse it. Locate it wherever shared UI lives in the project.

### 5. Hand it over

Surface the URL (and the `?variant=` keys). The user will flip through whenever they get to it. The interesting feedback is usually **"I want the header from B with the sidebar from C"**, which is the actual design they want.

### 6. Capture the answer and clean up

Once a variant has won, capture the answer (which variant and why), then capture the prototype the way the [SKILL](SKILL.md) describes. Fold the winner into the real code and move the rest onto the throwaway branch, not into main:

- **Sub-shape A**: fold the winner into the existing page; drop the losing variants and the switcher from main.
- **Sub-shape B**: promote the winning variant to a real route; drop the throwaway route and the switcher from main.

The full set of variants is the primary source, so it lands on the throwaway branch, not the bin, since variant components and the switcher left in the main branch rot fast and confuse the next reader.

## Anti-patterns

- **Variants that differ only in colour or copy.** That's a tweak, not a prototype. Real variants disagree about structure.
- **Sharing too much code between variants.** A shared `<Header>` is fine; a shared `<Layout>` defeats the point. Each variant should be free to throw out the layout.
- **Wiring variants to real mutations.** Read-only prototypes are fine. If a variant needs to mutate, point it at a stub: the question is "what should this look like", not "does the backend work".
- **Promoting the prototype directly to production.** The variant code was written under prototype constraints (no tests, minimal error handling). Rewrite it properly when you fold it in.

- **B: Preact** (preact + @preact/signals), client-rendered from an empty shell.

content.text: what about astro?

Astro is a good fit for part of SurveyBeat, but I doubt it helps the answer page much. Here's my reasoning.

**What Astro is good at:** it builds pages to static HTML with no JavaScript by default, and adds small interactive "islands" only where needed. Its strength is pages whose content is known at build time or on the server.

**Why that strength mostly doesn't apply to the answer page:**
- **The server can't render the content.** The token sits after the `#` in the URL, so the server never sees it when the page loads (ADR 0005, done for privacy). The Pulse name, the Questions and the anonymity statement arrive only after the page POSTs the token to the Submission Worker. So Astro can only produce a static shell plus an interactive island.
- **Variants A and B already test that shape.** Variant A is a static HTML shell with a little plain TypeScript, and variant B uses Preact. With Astro, the page would be the same shell, built by another tool. I'd expect the numbers to come out close to A or B.
- **It adds a second build system.** ADR 0008 has one Vite project with two entries (the app and the answer page), sharing tokens, CSS, Schemas and strings. Astro runs on Vite underneath, but it would be its own app package with its own config, and the shared code would have to cross that boundary.

**Where Astro fits:** SPEC §5.8's **marketing landing page, pricing placeholder and legal pages** (privacy, terms, data processing agreement). Those are content pages, which is exactly what Astro is for. They are out of scope for this ticket. I'd record "use Astro for the marketing and legal site" as a candidate when that work comes up, rather than decide it now.

I can also add **variant E (Astro static page with a small island)** to the running prototype, so the answer-page claim is measured rather than argued. It costs an extra build setup in the prototype. Should I add it, or leave Astro for the marketing site?

**If you mean Vite itself:** it's already in. ADR 0008 makes `apps/web` one Vite 8 project with two entries, the app and the answer page. All four prototype variants are built with Vite 8. Astro would only add a layer on top of Vite.

Results from the prototype: the same answer screens, built four ways and measured with Lighthouse 13 as a mid-range phone on slow 4G (CPU slowed 4×, 5 runs each). FCP is when the page first draws anything. LCP is when the Question text appears, and that's the paint that counts here.

| **A** prerendered HTML + plain TS | 25 KB | 1 | **618 ms** | **1,120 ms** |

- **Effect Schema is most of A's JavaScript:** 23.5 KB of its 25 KB. Without Schema, A's script is 1.5 KB.

Base directory for this skill: /home/ubuntu/.claude/skills/grilling

Interview the user relentlessly until you reach a shared understanding. Map this as a **design tree**: every decision branches into the decisions that hang off it.

Work the tree in **rounds**. The **frontier** is every decision whose prerequisites are already settled: the questions you can ask _now_ without guessing at answers you haven't heard yet. Ask the whole frontier in one round: number each question and give your recommended answer. Then wait for the user's answers before the next round.

Format a round like so:

```
❓ **Q1** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>

---

❓ **Q2** - **<question title>**: <question body, might be multiple paragraphs, including multiple choices>

➡️ <your recommended answer>
```

Word each question so "yes" accepts your recommended answer.

Each round the user answers reshapes the tree: settled decisions push the frontier outward and unblock questions that depended on them. Recompute the frontier and ask the next round. A question whose answer depends on another question still open in this round belongs to a _later_ round, not this one.

Finding _facts_ is your job, never the user's. When a frontier question needs a fact from the environment (filesystem, tools, etc.), dispatch a sub-agent with a fresh context window to find it; don't ask the user for anything you could look up yourself. Don't block on it: a running exploration is an unsettled prerequisite, so only the questions downstream of it wait for the sub-agent to report; ask the rest of the frontier now. The _decisions_ are the user's: put each to them and wait.

The session is done when the frontier is empty: every branch of the design tree visited, nothing left silently assumed. Do not act on it until the user confirms you have reached a shared understanding.

# Domain Modeling

Actively build and sharpen the project's domain model as you design. This is the *active* discipline: challenging terms, inventing edge-case scenarios, and writing the glossary and decisions down the moment they crystallise. (Merely *reading* `GLOSSARY.md` for vocabulary is not this skill: that's a one-line habit any skill can do. This skill is for when you're changing the model, not just consuming it.)

## File structure

Most repos have a single context:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/
│       ├── 0001-event-sourced-orders.md
│       └── 0002-postgres-for-write-model.md
└── src/
```

If a `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` exists at the root, the repo has multiple contexts. The map points to where each one lives:

```
/
├── GLOSSARY-MAP.md
├── docs/
│   └── adr/                          ← system-wide decisions
├── src/
│   ├── ordering/
│   │   ├── GLOSSARY.md
│   │   └── docs/adr/                 ← context-specific decisions
│   └── billing/
│       ├── GLOSSARY.md
│       └── docs/adr/
```

Create files lazily: only when you have something to write. If no `GLOSSARY.md` exists, create one when the first term is resolved. If no `docs/adr/` exists, create it when the first ADR is needed.

## During the session

### Challenge against the glossary

When the user uses a term that conflicts with the existing language in `GLOSSARY.md`, call it out immediately. "Your glossary defines 'cancellation' as X, but you seem to mean Y. Which is it?"

### Sharpen fuzzy language

When the user uses vague or overloaded terms, propose a precise canonical term. "You're saying 'account': do you mean the Customer or the User? Those are different things."

### Discuss concrete scenarios

When domain relationships are being discussed, stress-test them with specific scenarios. Invent scenarios that probe edge cases and force the user to be precise about the boundaries between concepts.

### Cross-reference with code

When the user states how something works, check whether the code agrees. If you find a contradiction, surface it: "Your code cancels entire Orders, but you just said partial cancellation is possible. Which is right?"

### Update GLOSSARY.md inline

When a term is resolved, update `GLOSSARY.md` right there. Don't batch these up: capture them as they happen. Use the format in [GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md](./GLOSSARY-FORMAT.md).

`GLOSSARY.md` should be totally devoid of implementation details. Do not treat `GLOSSARY.md` as a spec, a scratch pad, or a repository for implementation decisions. It is a glossary and nothing else.

### Offer ADRs sparingly

Only offer to create an ADR when all three are true:

1. **Hard to reverse**: the cost of changing your mind later is meaningful
2. **Surprising without context**: a future reader will wonder "why did they do it this way?"
3. **The result of a real trade-off**: there were genuine alternatives and you picked one for specific reasons

If any of the three is missing, skip the ADR. Use the format in [ADR-FORMAT.md](./ADR-FORMAT.md).

I've claimed **[Slice Release 1 into implementation issues](https://github.com/chrisdoc/surveybeat-next/issues/18)**. Before cutting issues, two things need settling: what happens to the eight areas still under Not yet specified on the map, and how the issues are structured. Round 1:

---

❓ **Q1** - **Hostnames and the sending domain**: This is the "Domains and email DNS" area.

➡️ All under `surveybeat.app`:
- `app.surveybeat.app`: the Main Worker, serving the app, the API, and the static answer page at `/a`.
- `submit.surveybeat.app`: the Submission Worker, which has all logging off.
- `notify.surveybeat.app`: a new Cloudflare Email Sending subdomain. It leaves your mail server, SES, and the root domain's strict SPF untouched.

The PR stages each get `pr-<n>.app.surveybeat.app` and `pr-<n>.submit.surveybeat.app`, set up through Alchemy. Whether WorkOS accepts wildcard redirect URLs for those stages gets checked in the sign-in issue.

`surveybeat.app` and `www` stay on Vercel until the R1 cutover, which is its own issue. That issue also cleans up the three conflicting DMARC records and the leftover Clerk records. It changes your DNS, so you confirm it before it runs.

---

❓ **Q2** - **Translations (i18n)**: This is the "i18n foundation" area.

➡️ Use a **small typed message catalog of our own**, shared by both entries. Each message is a flat key with an `{placeholder}` template. Plurals, dates, and numbers use the browser's built-in `Intl` APIs. There is no i18next or FormatJS, because the answer page's 10 KB budget rules them out. English ships in R1. A test fails if a user-facing string isn't in the catalog.

---

❓ **Q3** - **How email templates are written**: This is the "Email templates" area.

➡️ Use **React Email**, rendered when the message is sent in the Queue-consumer Worker. React is already in the app stack, React Email handles the hard email-client and dark-mode details, and that Worker has no tight bundle budget. A snapshot test renders every template. Before release we do one manual check in Gmail, Outlook, and Apple Mail, in light and dark mode. Templates live in `packages/emails`.

---

❓ **Q4** - **Design system baseline**: This is the "Design system baseline" area.

➡️ **Tailwind CSS v4 plus Base UI** for the app. Design tokens are CSS custom properties, and the answer entry's inline CSS uses the same tokens. Charts are **hand-built SVG with a table view next to each chart**. R1 has only trend lines and distribution bars, so a chart library isn't worth it. The baseline is one small set of components: button, field, radio group, dialog, table, and chart.

---

❓ **Q5** - **Areas decided inside their implementation issue**:

➡️ These four are local design choices that block nothing upstream:
- the **D1 index schema**;
- **what a stored Result contains**;
- **the per-request session check and revocation** (a deny check plus the Membership, with a 5-minute access token);
- **the CI job layout and its secrets**.

Each one becomes an "open choice, with these constraints" section in the issue that builds it. The implementer decides it there and writes it down in the PR. Once Q1–Q5 are settled, nothing stays under Not yet specified.

---

❓ **Q6** - **Where the implementation issues live**: The map's tickets carry only `wayfinder:` labels.

➡️ Create a **"Release 1" tracking issue** (not a child of the map). All implementation issues are its **sub-issues**, with **native blocked-by links**, a `release-1` label, and the **"Release 1" milestone**. Each issue has:
- a goal;
- acceptance criteria;
- the ADRs it follows;
- the tests it adds, including privacy tests;
- open choices;
- what it's out of scope for.

The map's last entry points to the tracking issue.

---

❓ **Q7** - **The slices**: There are 15. Each is sized for one agent session, in dependency order:

| # | Issue | Blocked by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Workspace and tooling**: packages, catalog, TS 7, oxlint plugin (boundary rule), oxfmt, Vitest, CI for typecheck, lint, and unit tests | – |

| 6 | **Questions, Template, Pulse editor**: the weekly team health Template, Dimensions, the R1 Question types, the Question version model, add/remove/reorder, the time estimate and the warning above 7 Questions | 4 |
| 7 | **Round lifecycle engine**: schedule table and alarm, every state, per-time-zone opens, the single close instant, creating the next Round, skip/pause/close/cancel, the daily repair cron, tests that rerun each job twice (ADR 0006) | 6 |

## Goal
Transactional email that is never sent twice and never fails silently.

## Acceptance criteria
- An `EmailSender` domain interface with a Cloudflare Email Sending adapter on the new sending subdomain `notify.surveybeat.app`, provisioned with Alchemy `Cloudflare.Email.SendingSubdomain`. Don't touch the apex SPF/DMARC or the existing mail and SES records.

""")

S[7] = dict(title="Round lifecycle engine in the Organization Durable Object", blocked=[6], adrs="0006", body="""
## Goal
Rounds run themselves: open per time zone, close once, compute, share, and create the next one, even if any job runs twice.

## Acceptance criteria
- A schedule table plus one alarm set to the earliest due job. Each job is an idempotent DO method that runs in the same transaction as its state change.
- States: Scheduled → Open → Closed → Ready → Shared (Ready moves straight to Shared in R1), plus Cancelled.
- Open happens at the first member's local send. Eligible members are frozen then. **One close instant: the latest member's send time plus the window.**
- The next Round is always Scheduled. It is created with the Pulse and again at each open, keyed by Pulse and planned open date.
- Lead controls:
  - skip any of the next 8 weeks (skipping the Scheduled week cancels it);
  - pause cancels the Scheduled Round, and an Open Round runs to its end;
  - close early (uninvited members are never invited);
  - cancelling an Open Round deletes its Submissions and Participation records.
- A Scheduled Round picks up Pulse changes. An Open Round never changes.
- IANA time zones. Local times are converted to UTC when scheduled. In a daylight-saving gap the time moves forward; in an overlap the first occurrence wins.
- The daily Cron repairs missing alarms.
- The close job enqueues result computation. The compute itself is slice 11, so use a stub here.

## Tests
Run every job twice and check nothing changes the second time. A Round spanning UTC−8 and UTC+9. A daylight-saving transition. Skip, pause, close, and cancel.
""")

- **Email templates:** React Email.
- **Design system:** Tailwind v4 with Base UI, and hand-built SVG charts that each come with a table.

  contents: read

# One run per pull request at a time, and never cancel a running deploy or destroy.
concurrency:
  group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: false

env:
  STAGE: pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN }}
  CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}

jobs:
  deploy:
    # Fork pull requests get no secrets.
    if: github.event.action != 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@73e46992e05b19abd31f2f3c20e0e7370d762115 # v6.1.1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .node-version
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Build the web app
        run: pnpm --filter @surveybeat/web build
      - name: Deploy the stage
        run: pnpm exec alchemy deploy infra/alchemy.run.ts --stage "$STAGE" --yes --no-input
      - name: Read back the Submission Worker's deployed settings
        run: pnpm check:observability --stage "$STAGE"
      - name: Smoke test
        run: node infra/scripts/smoke.ts "https://$STAGE.app.surveybeat.app" "https://$STAGE.submit.surveybeat.app"

  destroy:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      # The head commit, because the merge ref is gone once the pull request is merged.
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@73e46992e05b19abd31f2f3c20e0e7370d762115 # v6.1.1
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .node-version
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm --filter @surveybeat/web build
      - name: Destroy the stage
        run: pnpm exec alchemy destroy infra/alchemy.run.ts --stage "$STAGE" --yes --no-input
